extracted.intended_audience: general readers and information/information-technology professionals concerned with information quality and management
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for identifying, characterising, and reducing 'information pollution' in digital and other communication contexts. Covers manifestations, causes, effects, and practical/technological/managerial solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of information pollution
rubrics_metrics.description: Information pollution (also referred to as info pollution) is the contamination of an information supply with irrelevant, redundant, unsolicited, hampering, and low-value information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include misinformation, disinformation, junk e-mail, and media violence. This definition sets the basic evaluative boundary for what counts as pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manifestation type — disruption vs damage to information quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The manifestations of information pollution can be classified into two groups: those that provoke disruption, and those that damage information quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disrupting pollutants: unsolicited electronic messages (spam), instant messages, mobile phone ringtones and interruptions, excessive labels on maps, readers ignoring newspapers' articles. Quality-damaging pollutants: inaccurate or outdated information, badly presented/unfocused/cluttered/wordy/poorly organised documents that make understanding difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Information should not be irrelevant or redundant; irrelevant and redundant content contaminates the information supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate communications for whether content is essential to the task/decision at hand; superfluous messages and unnecessary labels distract and increase pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Information quality requires accuracy and up-to-dateness; inaccurate or outdated information is a form of information pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to laws/regulations/handbooks that have changed and sources that have fallen behind—these can misinform the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and presentation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Information must be well presented: focused, clear, and well organised; poor presentation reduces information quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cluttered, wordy, unfocused or poorly organised documents make it difficult for readers to understand and therefore contribute to pollution; improving writing and presentation practices can minimise effects on others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume and overload (information overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: An abundance of available information (regardless of quality) can harm decision-making—information overload is a related concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cognitive studies show limited processing capacity; excessive volume leads to deterioration of decision quality, anxiety, decision paralysis, and stress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity of pollution
rubrics_metrics.description: The level and type of information pollution depend on context; what is polluting in one context may be acceptable in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: e-mail is more polluting in corporate settings, mobile phones are particularly disruptive in confined shared spaces like train carriages; evaluate medium × context when assessing pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural and commercial practices (cultural pollution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural practices such as continual advertising and mass publishing contribute to 'cultural pollution' by increasing distracting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norms like 'you cannot have too much information' and industry practices of printing/distributing regardless of demand increase volume and make distinguishing valuable information harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological design choices to reduce interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology that creates frequent interruptions should be replaced with less-'polluting' options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and select technologies to minimise unwanted interruptions (e.g., notification management); technology can also improve presentation quality to aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of decision support systems and dashboards for prioritisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology-based alternatives include decision support systems and dashboards that enable prioritisation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt information-prioritising tools to surface essential facts and reduce the effective noise reaching decision-makers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information management policies and integrity assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Management techniques such as e-mail usage policies and information integrity assurance strategies can mitigate information pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisational policies set expectations for communication volume and format; integrity assurance strategies help ensure that published/used information remains high quality and current.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time and stress management to minimise interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal management techniques—time management and stress management—help reduce the impact of information pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set priorities, minimise interruptions, and manage attention to reduce overload and its negative effects on task performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve writing and presentation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Improved writing and presentation practices can minimise information pollution effects on others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise focused content, clarity, and organisation to prevent documents and communications from becoming polluting noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an information management paradigm (information ecology / environmental parallel)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need for development of an information management paradigm that parallels environmental management practices—treating information pollution analogously to environmental pollution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply systemic, ecosystem-style thinking (information ecology) and filtering systems to manage information flows at scale rather than only ad hoc fixes.
